newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea keeps up pressure on union leaders.
newsitem.headline: South Korea keeps up pressure on union leaders.

text.p: South Korean police on Friday kept a security net around a Seoul cathedral where a top strike leader was hiding from arrest, and the ruling camp scoffed at the fugitive's acceptance of an offer for a televised debate.
Groups of special force officers trained in unarmed combat guarded approaches to Myongdong cathedral in central Seoul.
The so-called "grabbers" -- hardened by years of street fighting -- are deployed during riots to rush into crowds and make arrests.

But by late evening, most uniformed riot police, who have regularly blocked workers trying to march on the cathedral, had pulled back. Some were keeping warm inside several buses stationed a few blocks away.
Earlier in the day, up to 1,000 riot police ringed the cathedral grounds.
South Korea's Roman Catholic cardinal appealed to President Kim Young-sam during a meeting to "resolve the current situation with dialogue", a presidential spokesman said.
In an unusual move, Catholic priests pitched a tent close to the fugitives' own ramshackle shelter.
"We pitched the tent to protect the union leaders," Father Park Kiho said, adding that a number of priests would sleep there until the crisis was resolved.

Strike leader Kwon Young-kil, president of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, challenged chairman of the ruling New Korea Party Lee Hong-koo to a public debate over the new labour law that has sparked more than three weeks of stoppages.

He was taking up Lee's own suggestion for a televised, round-table discussion between New Korea Party leaders and unspecified union heads about the law that allows companies to dismiss workers and replace strikers.
Kwon called on Lee to personally square off with him on camera. He also said the government must guarantee his safety from arrest.
But the New Korea Party spurned the offer on the grounds that Kwon was a fugitive, and called on unions to put forward more suitable candidates.
"Even for a television debate, the law should be observed," a New Korea Party statement said. "There cannot be guarantees of safety for people who have legal problems."
Kwon later said he would be prepared to hold the televised debate with Lee at Myongdong cathedral.
He and six deputies are all evading arrest at the church, directing industrial action with portable telephones.

In a further sign the strikes have wound down and only pockets of worker resistance remain, Hyundai Motor Co Ltd, the country's largest carmaker, said it would reopen its plants on Saturday after a week of temporary shutdowns.

The Labour Ministry said strikes were tapering off, with only 57,320 workers at 48 companies involved. The confederation put the figure at up to 200,000 and vowed to continue partial strikes in public services and manufacturing.
Kwon had insisted that a debate did not imply his union was seeking dialogue over the law.
Wrangling over the debate indicated both sides were jockeying for position in a battle for public opinion.

Public support for the government was wavering, with many commentators comparing President Kim to past strongman rulers for the way legislation that transforms South Korea's industrial landscape was rammed through parliament.
The law was passed in a dawn sitting of parliament on December 26 while opposition deputies slept.

In what is widely viewed as an ominous warning of a crackdown, authorities have linked labour strife to North Korea and produced communist propaganda from Pyongyang they say is circulating among strikers.
The two Koreas have been technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.
